text: Kabul is my current favorite restaurant in Philadelphia, and probably the best Afghan restaurant I've ever been to. It's a popular spot that fills up quickly on weekend evenings. The atmosphere is warm and inviting, even romantic - but what keeps me coming back is the food. From the appetizer list, try the Bulanee Gandana and Bulanee Kadu - fried turnovers filled with scallions and herbs, and delicately spiced pumpkin, respectively. They remind me of fried wontons. The complimentary salad is rather unpretentious - iceberg lettuce and sliced cucumber, with a few carrot shavings tossed in. The dressing makes it special, though. It's a zingy, tangy, yogurt-based concoction that tastes of garlic, mint, and I think cilantro... very tasty. The menu boasts many vegetarian entrée options, which makes me very happy. One favorite is the Norenge Palaw - chunks of eggplant simmered with tomatoes and spices, covered by a mound of sweet, cardamom-scented saffron rice, and topped with almonds, pistachios, and slivers of candied orange zest. Another favorite is the Chalaw Lobya - kidney beans simmered with onions in a wonderfully spiced tomato sauce, then topped with a touch of yogurt and a dash of green powder, which I think may be finely ground mint leaves; this dish is served with a plate of deliciously spiced white or brown basmati rice. I also love the Chalaw Sabzi - spinach cooked with kidney beans and spices, with a touch of tomato, also served with white or brown basmati rice. Another winning dish is Facillya - green beans cooked with onions in a tomatoey sauce. This dish is more subtly spiced than some of the others, but it's a bit spicier in heat level. Not hot, mind you; just enough to make it interesting. Simple and flavorful. This is home-style cooking at its best. Luckily they also bring you Afghan bread, kind of the Middle Eastern version of focaccia; it's perfect to sop up all that delicious sauce. And if you can't choose from the lovely selection, don't fret - you can order side dishes of most vegetable dishes for $4! If you have room for dessert, do try the Sheer-E-Yakh - vanilla ice cream topped with almonds, pistachios, and a pink rosewater-flavored syrup. It's divine. For the record: I have dined here with omnivorous friends as well, and they've all proclaimed the meat dishes to be as tasty as the veggie fare. Also, a note on the prices: Yes, they are a bit high when you look at the food-per-dollar ratio. But honestly, the food is so well prepared and so extremely flavorful, that I still feel it's worth every penny. And I have never, ever left this place still hungry. In fact, I always end up with a container of leftovers to take home and enjoy the next day.

text: I'm trying to find an excellent Chinese take-out place in the Palm Harbor area, and haven't had much success. So I'm working my way through all the Yelp listings I haven't tried yet. I stopped in for supper at China Taste with a family member after receiving a flyer on my doorstep from them. China Taste is located in the Boot Ranch shopping center between Target and Publix. The dining room has a few tables available for eating-in, and the room was clean and neat. Order taking was prompt, and the food arrived quickly. I ordered a chicken & shrimp with broccoli special, and switched the pork fried rice to chicken, and my guest ordered a standard chicken and broccoli combo meal. I added egg roll and wonton soup, and my guest's combo came with egg roll. As for the food, I found it uninspiring. In other cities I usually find it hard to be disappointed with Chinese take-out food. I'm not sure why, but I've found very few really good places in the Clearwater/Palm Harbor area, with the average place here below most other cities I've lived/spent time in. I say all of that to emphasize my expectations here for Chinese take-out are pretty low. But China Taste failed to meet even these lowered expectations. I found the wonton soup flavorful, but nothing remarkable. The egg roll was a bit overdone, and had very little flavor. The chicken fried rice was bland and lacked any significant flavors or seasonings. On balance, the chicken & shrimp and broccoli flavors were a bit better and well-cooked, but nothing to rave about. As for value, the portions for everything were ample, and I was only able to eat about half of my meal. When the food is great, it's a bonus to take home leftovers. When the food is not so great and the leftovers got thrown away, it simply makes the meal more expensive. I won't be going back to China Taste, and that was echoed by my guest. My scores, on my "Chinese-take-out" scale : Atmosphere: 3 Service: 4 Food: 2 Value: 2 I'm moving on my next target, Big Bok Choy Bistro on Tampa Rd. in Oldsmar.

text: Much fanfare had been given on the Internet about the burgers at Good Dog, a bar located on 15th street between Walnut and Locust, especially in regards to their Good Dog burger which comes stuffed with Roquefort cheese. I opted for their traditional burger, prepared medium - which is how I ask for all my burgers. Medium gives you just the right amount of pink for it to be juicy, but not still mooing. I came during the lunch hour on a Friday, so it was full but not packed and I sat at the bar. And waited. And waited. When I was at the point of gnawing my arm off I was so hungry, my burger finally arrived on - SURPRISE! - a brioche bun! (But that was on the menu so I guess I already expected that. Plus, I could tell by everyone else getting served their food before me.) Their fries came with a side of their housemade aioli for dipping. It was kind of like a watery version of the onion ring sauce at Burger King. I prepared to dive into this delicious burger, my palate poised to receive the succulent, juicy meat. But, lo and behold after first bite, I realized not only was my burger not even the slightest bit of pink in the middle (it was hard to tell at first in the dim lighting of the bar), but it was dry, overcooked and charred - lettuce, tomato and ketchup used as an attempt to cover up the grill marks. I was starving so there was no way I was sending it back at this point and so, I trudged on and chewed through the meat like a dog chewing on rawhide. I was extremely disappointed. No flavor, just the taste of burnt beef in my mouth. And let's not even get into the brioche bun being used yet again in a completely unoriginal attempt to fancy-ify this overpriced bar burger. ($11?? Seriously??) Regardless of how busy your kitchen is, the least you can do is try to prepare food to your customer's request. I can only imagine what would have happened if I ordered a steak there (if they even serve steak; I have no clue.) Or if I had some kind of food allergy. (I actually think I did have some allergic reaction to whatever was in their aioli after I left. I've never known myself to have food allergies before, but my throat felt like it was closing up and made it hard to swallow.) I guess they just figured it was better to overcook my burger then undercook it, and that does not a good burger make. Bad dog, very bad dog.

text: The following update is my response to the owner's comment on my previous review. My review does deserve some tweaking based on her feedback. In my review, I referenced a lactation consultant and used inappropriate language to describe her. That language has no place on sites like Yelp, no matter how funny I think it might be at the time. My reviews, in general, are truthful representations of my experiences of businesses in the St. Louis area (as evidenced by my wide range of ratings and array of types of businesses I have reviewed). Sometimes I employ foul language and descriptors to make my reviews more memorable to a reader. However, I realize that, in this case, my use of foul language came from a place of anger and not from a place of wanting to review this business. For that, I am truthfully sorry and have amended my previous review to reflect these changes. I have also taken out any part where I encouraged the reader to not use the services provided at this business because this was MY experience, but everyone is entitled to their own. I entered his place of business seeking out an expert in a time where I was worried about my child, and I was met with eye rolling and general rudeness. In addition, I wanted her expert advice and yet the advice she gave me was nothing more than breast feeding tips I could have gotten from any Google search. While Kellymom.com is a popular source, I don't think you can fully trust any information you find on the internet. This review included. I also felt I received absolutely no breast feeding encouragement from the lactation consultant I spoke with and encouragement is what any mother (breast feeding or not) needs above all else. If I would have received an answer I didn't want to hear, but it was framed in a supportive and encouraging way, I probably could have given this a five-star review. Even if I didn't "like" the advice or "hear what I wanted to hear." And though I do feel that the response to my review came from a place of trying to protect her business, I do not appreciate the insinuation that I exaggerated this interaction. Like I said in the review, I had a friend with me at the time and she also thought the lactation consultant's approach was rude. Additionally, I was NEVER asked the age of my child (not one time, not several times, ZERO times). I know this to be true because the response indicated I was asking a question about my daughter - but I don't have a daughter, I have a son. As always, when you are reading any reviews (or responses to the reviews, for that matter) remember that they are always based on one person's experience usually based on one visit. Feel free to use the reviews to guide you in your choices, but also feel free to completely ignore them and do what is best for you.

text: I am very sorry, I do not give 1 star without consideration - people invest their lives in their businesses and those businesses employ many people. that said however... in the end my loyalty is first to the Yelp community. There are differing standards of excellence by different reviewers - a bar by a college will likely be ranked differently then a staid white tablecloth place in an upper middle class neighborhood (notice how no one called themselves rich - after all we ALL deserve tax breaks right?). I might be a tough reviewer but I ate at 5 Brothers in Reading PA and was very impressed - I would give them a 3. This place is just disappointing. Don't go here unless you are a kid or looking to score points with or mollify a kid, or if you are attempting to curry some sort of favor with someone who demands to go here for whatever reason.. One enters Jake's and is assailed by Mix 106 (106.1 FM) at a loud level. Yeah I am getting old but I will still rock out - yet a constant loud booming radio playing is not conducive to a decent meal. It might be fast food, however I think only the 15-25 YO cohort will enjoy the musical barrage - eating should be relaxing not stressful! The king of steaks, Steve's Prince of Steaks ( http://www.yelp.com/biz/steves-prince-of-steaks-philadelphia#hrid:U3ssbZbW8EOv8GAhuaQHdw/src:self ) encloses their grill in the back room with windows that allow patrons of my liege to observe the royal minions at work. Five guys has the grill well back from the dining area with a high glass wall, Tony Luke's, like the Prince has the cooking behind glass. Jake's has the cooking out in the open with minimal partitions. Yeah you can closely monitor the work of the cooks - just like at places with glass partitions. The smell of cooking burgers, appetizing at first, but tiresome after a few moments permeates the place. The menu is extensive, and my dining companion and I had 2 burger deals - for most folks a single would be fine. The burgers were greasy and sorry,just not as good as Five Guys - Jake's burgers were just OK. I think they might have been cooked at too high a temperature but were not dried out. The fries were lovely to behold but when one bit into them they were mealy - for 2 bucks I am paying for good fries and they should deliver. The onion rings were at first very nice, but upon first bite it became obvious that they consist of nicely cooked breading with a minimal filing of onion. The shakes were nicely hand prepared but the ice cream and/or the syrup employed in the crafting of the shake were substandard with the product fully equal to the ingredients. There was a movie where I think Paul Newman played a bar tender at a place. He was having an argument with the owner and to illustrate his opinion of the management of the place he says '...one day I had a steak here and it was not good. A steak is either good or not good...' - all that the chef does is to cook it. If a steak is not good it's because the quality simply was not there. Jake's could be much better with a few changes: 1) Music is fine, but at a lower volume - if the manager can't hear it in the back don't crank it, go to Best Buy 1 mile down the street and buy an additional speaker for the back and 50 feet of wire! 2) It's the ingredients, people! What's the hallmark of great cooking? Simple preparations of the best freshest meats and produce available. A better level of meat, fries, ice cream, and rings would go a long, LONG way. 3) Proper cooking! many many years ago I worked at McDonald's. The grills and friers were checked for proper temperature by managers who carefully calibrated their thermometers. Oil was sucked out of the frier and color checked against a calibrated plastic sample. If the oil was dirtier then the sample it was done. McDonald's had huge standardized buying - if Jake's does then that's a big problem. 'Quality is our recipe'. Yeah not the best burgers, but hey they do a good burger for a decent price, and I think that on the day i visited Jake's Wendie's would have been better. A lot better. 4) Put a glass wall up to keep the kitchen smells in the kitchen! Just build a waist high wall and top it off with glass so folks can see the clean kitchen that they have at Jake's. The people were nice, the place and the bathrooms were clean, the dining room was very clean - they do all the secondary stuff get the food up to snuff!

text: Holy mackerel! Or snapper! Or Tuna! Or Eel! All You Can Eat Lunch for $12.99!!! We weren't sure if this was too good to be true, but we figured we'd give it a try. Only certain items are on the All You Can Eat (AYCE) order sheet, but there are quite a few options above your standard Spicy Tuna roll or Cucumber Roll. Usually, for lunch specials, you always get stuck with the basic fish-and-rice-only sushi - no eggs, crunch, mayo, tempura, etc. That is NOT the case here. And there are several sushi (fish over bed of rice, non-roll) to choose from as well. I had the crab, shrimp, and eel - all very good. Eel was the best. Also listed on the AYCE sheet are appetizers, such as Miso Soup, Salad w/ Ginger Dressing, 2pc Crab Rangoon, 3pc Gyoza pot sticker, shrimp shumai, etc. So I came in for lunch, ordered my drink, grabbed the little sheet, and marked 2 sushi and 2 rolls, and 1 appetizer. The appetizer came out pretty quickly. While we were finishing, I marked up the sheet again for another mini-appetizer and 2 pcs of sushi. By the time I finished my last bites, two of the items had been delivered. So the pacing was good, and you didn't wait long at all. Service was very friendly. We were still surprised to see $12.99 on our receipt - still thought it was too good to be true. Watch for the coupons on the website for another $2 off. I think my soda was $1.75. GREAT VALUE! WE WILL DEFINITELY BE BACK.

text: This is my favorite restaurant. This place has the best sushi in Indiana hands down. The fish is always fresh, the rolls are unique and brilliantly blend a variety of distinct flavors together for an unforgettable taste. An example is the corona roll, it has spicy tuna, avacado and crunchy tempura chips on the inside, and white tuna, wasabi mayo, and slices of lime on the top. The ingredients in the roll work well together to create a delicious roll which has a very faint corona-like taste (Mainly because of the lime, it does not taste like beer or alcohol at all). Another roll, which happens to be my favorite is the playboy roll. The inside of the roll is stuffed with tempura shrimp, asparagus, spicy tuna, and some of those crunchy tempera flakes. The roll is topped with cooked shrimp and 3 special sauces. But what really brings the playboy roll alive and distinguishes it from other rolls is the way it is cooked before it reaches your table. After the playboy roll is rolled, it is wrapped in aluminum foil and placed on a plate with everclear (a flammable alcohol). The server then sets the everclear on fire, creating a flame under the sushi that cooks it while it is wrapped in aluminum foil. The server drops the playboy roll off on your table while it is still on fire. After the fire is gone and the roll is cooked, open up the foil and be prepared for the best taste of you life. Aside from the sushi, Naked Tchopstix has excellent other food also. I recommend the spicy sashimi mix, the toast and jam, and the pot stickers.

text: I came here last night after arriving late on a long and tumultuous bus ride. I had always heard about Monk's, the mussels, and the beer list, but never had the opportunity or time to check it out. When I finally did, it was life changing. First, the beer list is phenomenal, albeit overpriced for Philly standards (most beers on tap are $8). Free from "lager", they feature a slate of regional and European craft beers, as well as many, many, many, many bottles from all over the world. And you have to read the beer bible if you can, if not for the humor and light-hearted approach to beer, for the informative lessons about how its made and the many different types. Even your beer snob buddies might learn a thing or two. Second, we knew it was clearly a foodie place when we got there after 10 and STILL had to wait for a table (much to the disbelief of some passerby). The wait at that point was pretty short, but it would all be worth it for the other main reason why you come here: The Mussels. You cannot get better mussels anywhere else in Philly. Why? Because you get a huuuuuge pot of gourmet mussels with fries and bread for $10. Seriously. It's like one of the city's best kept foodie secrets. And they're really good mussels too. I had the Ghent mussels (amazingly savory with bacon, bleu cheese, leeks, fume, and simmered in Saison Dupont), while he had the Red Light (Hoegaarden Broth with spicy chili peppers, chervil, and garlic). Why do more people not take advantage of this amazing deal? Apparently, they have really good burgers too, but that'll be for the return trip. For now, this was hands down one of the best, if not the best dinner I've had in a really long time in Philly.

text: Just as a disclaimer, I booked this room a week before graduation weekend in Santa Barbara because there wasn't anything else available. I'd never been to a Motel 6 before, but I thought, "How bad could it be?" The day my girlfriend and I were supposed to check in, I called the motel in the afternoon just to make sure we could come later since my reservation confirmation didn't have a check-in time. "Best Wester -- Motel 6?" was how they answered. Strike one. Then, as I tried to ask my question, they cut me off and bluntly said, "We don't have any cancellations for tonight. Is that your question?" Strike 2. I tried to let them know that we were coming in later and I wanted to make sure that was okay. They responded with, "Listen, I've got a line full of customers here. We will be here when you get here!", and then the phone went dead. I was so stunned at how rude this person was. Strike three. We ended up arriving at 11:30 that evening because we had spent the whole day in Santa Barbara with my family. We got the key and the person at the front desk let me know they charged my card already at 6:00pm. So, we went to the room, opened the door, and it reeked of cigarette smoke -- even though I specifically reserved a non-smoking room. Strike four. My girlfriend has asthma and she was already feeling the effects from the stench. We tried to open the window to let some fresh air in, but it only opened three inches. Once we found the cigarette burns on the bed spread, we decided there was no way we could stay here. Strike 5. We went down to the person at the front desk, described the situation, and the best they could offer was a partial credit for a "no show." No show? Not only did we show up, but we didn't have the non-smoking room that we paid for. Strike 6. They didn't have any other rooms available, so we ended up driving back up to Santa Barbara and sleeping on our friend's floor at 1:00am. The next day I called the General Manager, told him the situation, including my girlfriend's health concerns, and he said the best he could offer was a 50% refund. I couldn't believe it. He wanted me to pay $58 for a room that was not only sub-par, but that I didn't even stay in! Strike 7. So, I called Guest Services of the Motel 6 Central Booking System to see if they would be more understanding. After being on hold for a few minutes, they said that there was nothing they could do, and that the refund was at the full discretion of the manger at the property. Strike 8. You would think that if a company wronged a customer it would be in their best interest to make sure I didn't feel ripped off! I was so furious with them because part of me knows that they could have done something to help me out. Later that day, I went back to the motel to try to speak to the manager one more time. Of course he wasn't there, and since I had to leave to go back home, I reluctantly took the 50% refund. As a young person with many more years of possible Motel 6 stays, you would think that $58 wasn't worth their reputation being tarnished by my bad experience. In the end, I felt like I was taking the loss when they were the ones that made the mistakes. I called my bank and disputed the charge (thank you Chase!), but in the end, I realize I was the one that made the mistake of booking a room at the Carpinteria South Motel 6.

text: I have never had a bad meal at Bandana's, you really can't go wrong choosing any of their smoked meats. I always wind up ordering a combo plate because I can never decide on just one meat. I like their dry rubbed ribs because they prove to be the perfect vehicle for getting the various bar-b-q sauces from the squeeze bottles on the table to my mouth. If you want a salad, they only have bar-b-q ranch or regular ranch dressing. We ordered the large nacho appetizer, sour cream and jalapenos are optional. They use real cheese on the nachos, not that creamy orange stuff that passes for cheese used at some places. The meat is shredded and in a bar-b-q sauce places on top of a pile of taco chips. I would order them again. My only complaint was with the service. Our appetizer was served and just as we were starting to eat it, our server brought out our main courses and placed them on the table. Now we have to decide which plate we are going to eat hot and which we will eat cold. This seems to happen all too often in many restaurants. perhaps it is my fault for giving the server our entire order and assuming she knew that we wanted to eat our appetizer BEFORE our main dish was served. For warned is for armed, if you don't want all of your meal piled on your table all at once, order your meal AFTER you have ordered and consumed your appetizers.

text: Dr. Kemp is an amazing orthodontist and runs a great practice. I had braces as a child, but let's just say the experience wasn't the best. Dr. Kemp fixed the "work" I'd had done previously by someone else. His office is conveniently located just off Mack Hatcher and across the road from the YMCA in Franklin. The waiting area is well-stocked with magazines, cozy chairs, and K-cups of coffee, hot tea, cocoa, etc. For the bathroom checkers, it's nothing but granite, high end fixtures and impeccable cleanliness; the polish and design that went into this building shows just how much they pay attention to detail. The building is nice, but the people are what sets the practice apart. His staff are all warm, friendly and professional. From your initial visit and consultation you will be treated as if you're an honored guest of the collective Kemp "family". You'll be surprised at how quickly you feel completely familiar and at ease. The orthodontic assistants are quick, gentle, and skilled. The layout of the operating room means you'll be in and out in no time; 10-20 chairs are arranged in a circle and then an overflow side area so that space isn't wasted. Dr. Kemp can go from chair to chair quickly for progress checks and adjustments. It's amazing how a few quick turns of a wire with tiny pliers can make my smile so perfect --and it IS perfect. The man is good at what he does. Oh and in case I forgot, he's also "orthodontist to the stars". His patients of note include several Titans, Predators, Country music stars, models, actors, etc. People who regularly injure their smile and people who make money with their smile all entrust their mandibular alignment to Dr. Kemp; why not you?
label: POS

text: I have been going to this spot since they opened but have not gone in awhile. Went for lunch yesterday and have to come back often. I had the special which was a sweet potato and black bean quesadilla with a "funky" slaw. The quesadilla was hot, crisp, seasoned just right. The potato was still intact and had a wonderful smooth texture and taste. The slaw was a standout with finely chopped veggies in a thyme vinagrette. The peppery taste of the veggies and the vinagrette worked perfectly together and went well with the smooth quesadilla. I ate every scrap and was sad there was not another plate of it on the table to finish off. We were seated right away and the server checked back with us several times. Husband had the melted cheese which was grilled and melted all the way through. He finished every bite also. Cost with two entrees and one drink around $30. Pricey for lunch but it is not every time I rave so much about a dish. Even the high end places have not made me as happy as this one plate of food did.

The place was clean, including the restroom. We will definitely return.

The better part of the meal was feeling like we were at a wonderful dinner party at the home of friends. Juliana & her husband both made sure to greet and chat with guests all evening. The dining room on the main floor is small and cozy and the background music is quiet enough to allow for lots of table-to-table talk to compare dishes and ooh & aah over desserts. text: Some thoughts: I initially found it very strange that so few of the Philadelphia- and New Jersey-area transit services I rode had Yelp listings. I guess I can understand each train line not having a listing yet, but Market East Station? So I spent a lot of time researching addresses, locations, and the like to make sure my First to Review reviews laid a good foundation for many useful, funny, cool reviews to come. And you know what happened? Within a day, the Yelp Philadelphia moderators (and whoever is in charge of Trenton) changed the titles of my listings. So my specific review of New Jersey Transit's Northeast Corridor Line magically turned into a review of "N J Transit"--and you know how much I hate needless spaces between initials--and my review of SEPTA's Trenton Line Regional Rail turned into a review of SEPTA. But that's stupid, because I had already reviewed SEPTA in a different review. So in the interest of making things simpler for its users, Philadelphia Yelp's moderators believe it's better to create duplicate listings. Really? Why would you go to the trouble of changing something as specific as a review of train line and not actually research whether what you're changing it to already exists? Actually, Philadelphia Yelp, I'd like to apply for a part-time job as a moderator. I'm really good at research and fact-checking, and I'm a public-transit geek. Back to Market East Station. It's subterranean. But unlike Radiohead's "Subterranean Homesick Alien," which is sad in a beautiful way, Market East Station is just sad. I didn't really feel homesick here, but I did feel like a kind of alien. Actually, I thought about Downtown L.A. in the mid-'80s and all that subterranean ridiculousness that was cool for all of three seconds and then became sad. And when I was doing research on Market East Station--because I really do research before I write reviews--I learned that the station opened in 1984, which partially explains why it reminded me of L.A.'s own crumbling underground attempts at revitalization. But I don't hate the place. It's actually a little comforting in an uncomfortable way, because discomfort can be familiar, and what we fear most is often the unknown, no matter how much better or easier or less stressful it can make our lives. What I'm really talking about are cellphones. And strange guys with neck tattoos who tell you, while you're waiting for your South Philly friend to call you back and/or pick you up, that Hurricane Irene is coming and that they've already evacuated Jersey. Even with my limited knowledge of local customs and jargon, I knew the guy was exaggerating. Evacuated Jersey? As in the entire state? I had just been there; and it didn't seem like 8,791,894 people were preparing for Armageddon. OK, maybe some of them were, but I didn't see them. So I gave Erin O./G. the agreed-upon fifteen minutes, waited another five, called her back, waited another five, and promptly found a taxi, which was very easy, by the way. The station seems really confusing. I didn't get confused, but I could see myself getting confused. It was very comforting waiting at the corner of 12th and Filbert, tattooed-neck guy's presence notwithstanding. (Actually, tattooed-neck guy was one of the least troubling of the people I ran into while waiting.) See, one of the people who laid out San Francisco's streets was from Philadelphia, so we have a Market Street, a Sansom Street (spelled differently), a Cherry Street, a Chestnut Street, and a Filbert Street! So while I waited near the corner of 12th and Filbert, I imagined myself on Filbert Street in San Francisco's Cow Hollow. That neighborhood is the furthest thing from scary, so it was fine. I'd like to visit this station many more times. And to partake of its subterranean-mall sadness. And to keep it going. Because the '80s were so hopeful for so many people even though they knew they were headed for the precipice. Kind of like 2007, actually.

text: First off, I am not a foodie or too cro-magnon like to appreciate a 10 course meal or too prissy to enjoy a street vendor, I like tasty food plain and simple - so take my review with a grain of salt. I had heard great things about Blackfish so I took my wife, picked up some nice wine, and expected a great meal and evening. One of the problems with this place I noticed immediately is it is PACKED! They squeeze way too many tables in there and I can appreciate atmosphere, but it was a little too intimate. Plus our table was in the middle of the foot traffic so servers and other diners were constantly walking next to and around our table. It seems like they are trying to cash in on every square foot possible, but for the price of the dinner it should decide if it wants to be fine dinning or a neighborhood restaurant - it can't be both. The food? Well - for starters I had the Hamachi. Decent, but bland and the sauce was oily and there was too much of it and it destroyed the delicate nature of Yellowtail. Kind of a small serving but hey it was the first course. My wife had a squash soup which again not great - it was runny and bland, not very rich and really not that exciting. I would have expected this kind of soup at Panera to be honest. For the second course - I had the Lobster. It was severely undercooked. Trust me. I grew up in Maine and I know what good lobster is and how not to overcook it, but this was almost raw. The tail is one of the toughest parts of the lobster to cook properly, but this was very rubbery and not very appealing. Again, the sauce was... not good and did not add to the dish and the size of the tail was about jumbo prawn. My wife had the fois gras, which was a homerun. Very tasty and without a doubt the best dish of the evening. I would eat that again. Third course - I had the duck. I love duck. I would eat Donald if I could. But this was not a good duck. Somehow the breast was medium rare in the inner part, but extremely dry on the outside. The only thing I could think of that it sat for too long and the juices bled out, which explains why that the third course took forever to arrive. The sauce was great, my only complaint was not having enough of it to mask the dryness of the duck. My wife had the sea bass which as blackened properly and good enough, but again - not very creative nor out of the ordinary. We each had a desert, which was ok - nothing to remember. I am not sure if they made them on site since the chocolate had a bit of sitting in a display case too long taste. We got the bill and as expected, spending $200 including tip - both of us felt extremely disappointed leaving the restaurant. I would say considering the amount of money, that was one of the worst meals I have had. Who knows? Blackfish is doing something right to gain all of the hype, but for the money I can think of many other places to go and at least get better atmosphere and good (not out of this world) food. If they could do more stuff like the fois gras - I would be back, but until then - adieu!

text: I'm not sure why, but several negative reviews of this restaurant have been flagged as inappropriate. La Cote Basque is, at best, a two star restaurant, and it's not a French restaurant at all. I have been to much, much better French restaurants, albeit some are in other cities. Read my reviews and you will see several others.. I don't know how this restaurant survives if it's trying to present itself as a French restaurant. There's hardly any authentic French food on this menu. It seems strongly influenced by German (Bratwurst, Saurkraut, Schnitzel) and Italian (Lasagna, Spaghetti, Eggplant Parm) but those aren't done well either. Where's the Osso Bucco? Where's the selection of various mussel recipes? Where's the Lamb Pappardelle? Or even some Frites with selection of flavored mayonaise? None of those are there. Before you go to this supposedly French restaurant, do yourself a favor and read the menu on their web site at http://www.lacotebasquewinehouse.com. I challenge you to find more than three or four French choices on the menu. I don't even know how to rate this as a French Restaurant because it's not French, and as an Italian restaurant or a German restaurant, I've had MUCH, MUCH better. If you want French in the St. Petersburg area, head over to St. Pete Brassiere in downtown St. Pete. Even Cassis American Brassiere is closer to French than this place. A side tip - don't go in the rain or you'll have to wade through the parking lot to and from your car. Your shoes, socks, and feet WILL get soaked if you go in the rain. This place is awesome; it has a great bar where you can sit and dine while holding great conversation and actually hear the person, the dining area is simple, ample spacing between tables and really provides privacy in your dining experience which so many restaurants have missed the mark on these days. First, the horses - the whole reason we were there, quite frankly. We learned about what it takes to maintain and show the horses - and saw for ourselves that they live in the lap of luxury (for a horse - it's all relative). I have to admit - their stable is probably cleaner than my house - very impressive operation. We then moved onto the manufacturing - which I thought would be boring. The presentation of the facts was done in a relevant way - and we were moved in and out of buildings at a good pace - the tour passed quickly. We went thru a number of buildings - each with wonderful things to look at: the beauty of the old buildings, all perfectly maintained; or the amazing technology in place. And the cleanliness is unbelievable! Last stop was the hospitality room in the same building we started. Breakfast Beer! At that point, we were back on our own to look at their memorabilia collection (including prohibition period) or the gift shop. A few notes: 1) Dress for the weather - you are going to be going to spend time walking outside between buildings. 2) Wear walking shoes - no flip flops, crocs etc. 3) Bring your camera 4) Not suitable for strollers, and I'm gonna say taking a toddler aged child on the tour is not ideal. Older kids (8 and up?) or babes in arms will do just fine. 5) My only complaint was the tour website - it vaguely states tours run from 10a to 4p - but it's not clear what time each tour starts - I suspect (but don't know) they start on the hour. All in all - very impressed by the facility and the company. Would I return: Yes Would I recommend: Yes - this is a must-do for anyone travelling to St. Louis, including families.

text: Okay, so the pizza is not empirically good, per se - but you know when you associate really, really pleasant memories with food, and by complete association of this foodstuff - when you eat it, it tastes so much better because of that association? The pizza, crust, sauce and cheese is generic, sauce veers towards sweet, and the whole lot can be really greasy at times, but it is perfect for what it is. The association? It was the pizza of 'yore, consumed by me in my younger years sometimes by the beach, sometimes in Newark - but this particular location holds a special place in my heart. Good memories galore. When times were simpler and when pizza was just that: Pizza. Like all other Grotto's, it has a long history in Delaware and it is super family friendly. You can bring all generations here, grab a basket of free popcorn on your way in - celebrate a kid's birthday - it's that kind of wholesome place . text: One night after The Wife moved back from Chicago she suggested we go to Potbelly for dinner. My response was something along the lines of, "Wtf is a Potbelly?" Stunned that I wasn't familiar with, like, the greatest sandwich shop in the known universe, duh, and saddened by the fact that chain had yet to add a link in Indianapolis, she spent the next four years extolling the virtues of Potbelly at every opportunity. Here's the skinny - in 1977, a couple starts selling sandwiches our of their antique shop and names the enterprise after an antique cylindrical style of oven. Fast forward 20 years and they sell the concept to a guy who turns it into a 200-shop chain. They mostly sell baked sandwiches with good ingredients and killer giardiniera relish, Zapp's chips, and cookies and shakes. And as of May 3, 2011, they are open for business in Indianapolis. After four years of hype it was going to be hard to impress me but my first Potbelly impression was strong. The sandwiches are good (I think. When you put giardiniera on anything it just tastes like something with giardiniera on it.), reasonably sized, and cheap for what you get - I walked out of there with dinner for two for less than I'd spend in Subway. I can't weigh in on whether Potbelly is the best sandwich shop in the known universe, but it's definitely the best option in the context of Subway, Jimmy John's, et al.

The ultra lounge and pool on the 9th floor is plush, trendy, and looks like something from a resort. This is the area I live in and it was my favorite when I was shopping. I don't see anything but the Zen garden with 24-hour flame fountains and water running, so it is an amazing escape when I sit on my patio. The fitness center is huge and plush with top-notch equipment. There are six TVs, and all the cardio equipment allows you to plug in headphones and listen to whichever TV you choose. There is also a smaller workout room on the 9th floor along with a hardwood studio that has mirrors and a TV for other type programs such as Yoga. It's worth coming to take a tour if you are interested in buying one of the remaining 100 of 400+ units before they are all gone. text: Simply one of the most wonderful, and unique restaurant experiences on the West coast in the 21st century. Whenever I have a visitor from overseas or the Bay Area, I bring them here, and they swoon. Have been going for 30 years. Rarely this place has an off night. Generally though, it's God Damn this place is good!!!! This is authentic food served European peasant farmer communal style in huge portions. You want tongue? giant lamb chops? chorizo? You won't be given a menu, just check the white board at the dining room entrance after you've been to the bar (a bar which conjures up War Time Spain...try the authentic specialty Picon Punch). Utterly addicting skinny greasy french fries piled high, very tasty salad, hard goat cheese. Wine, bread, beans, salad, fries, side dish, comes with the meals. I don't eat soup except here (add pepper and hot sauce to it). There is always a cold bottle of unlabeled red wine on the table and it's really good! The authentic 1930s vintage Dive vibe (you'll think you're in an old Untouchables movie set... Joe Friday would like it here). It's a secret spot tourists have no clue about, but you'll see the local doctors and congressmen here. Don't be surprised to find grand old Reno patrician families of 12 or 15 or 20 eating here on a Sunday night. I've recently seen a Pulitzer prize winner feasting his family, and a Dutch hero of WWII resistance celebrating his 91st birthday here. The Santa Fe is a jewel that refused to sell out to the corporate Goliaths surrounding it (and that wasn't easy).

Plus I do love sequins! I took a group of locals to the museum for a day trip. A few things, in list form: The 1st floor: 1. We were the only ones there (there was seven of us) 2. One of the four staff we would eventually see, was sitting at her desk in a back room, not at the front desk. 3. The first floor is cavernous, and I mean it has a semi "empty" feeling. There are less than five mannequins on display. And a large replica of Smarty Jones. Not sure where that is fitting in with the theme. 4. No pamphlets or map to direct us, but overall it could pass as self guided experience. 5. There is rolling TV playing a video of performances, no commentary about the clubs performing, what they are performing, or any information in general. The organization of the first floor should be considered. The 2nd floor: There is no music playing at all on the 2nd floor. Isn't' that what the Mummers are known for? Music would set the tone of the experience for the museum. 1. It's dated and dusty. There doesn't seem to be much attention to the upkeep of the displayed costumes, which should be the biggest draw to the museum. The costumes were dusty or falling apart. They were ID'd, but should have been displayed in yearly progression for fluidity. 2. Over half of the interactive displays did not work. Including a Terminator display, a marching route map display, and fact board display. One particular exhibit had ear cones? to listen to, the sign stating "temporarily under maintenance" was dated and folding over itself. Apparently "temporary means 'indefinite'" 3. There is a large show room of props and costumes as well as places to sit, but it's amateurish, obviously neglected area. 4. You can try on Mummer's costumes in one exhibit. That was a lot of fun, definitely a plus. They only had adult sizes though, they should have children sizes as well since they have children participate in the parade. 5. All the pictures on display are from the 70's and 80's. Nothing to show progression in the 21st century. 6. There is information about how the Mummers came to be and some of their activities which was nice and informative. Lower Level: 1. Large event area 2. It has a stage 3. There are BINGO groups that meet there, which I think could be turned into a great money maker if organized right. Overall suggestions: 1. More Costumes on display, in progressive, yearly order 2. Weekly/monthly maintenance of the exhibits 3. Fix the displays 4. Play music upstairs 5. Have interactive family style, BINGO games involving dressed up Mummers with hot dogs/soda, and music to help raise money for the museum. 6. Update display pictures to reflect current events 7. More interactive media demonstrating the different groups, what they do, and how they set themselves apart from everyone else.

text: I'll say it: I'd switch teams for John Besh. Our bartender friend informed us that this particular burger was chosen as 8th in the nation; I'm not sure by whom, but I'm not mad I got it, just mad I'm not on the committee. We were told that they do them a bit differently than most places; as far as I can tell, they just cook the shrimp perfectly, and make the sauce good enough to drink. I was a bit disappointed that the fries were cooked past crispy into crunchy territory, but the lady on my left loved them all the same. For me though, the only downsides were said fries and the fact that their bloody mary is merely a mix (although I do like the Gator Blood), and they don't provide a spicy bean. text: In previous reviews I have mentioned our willingness to give second chances--in fact I have been known to re-review a once negative review with a more recent, positive one based on such a go-round. Sometimes I'll even go so far as the "three-strikes-and-you're-out" rule because I can't help but try and be optimistic. If that's what you came to find here, turn back now. This is unfortunately NOT one of those reviews. I had a mediocre experience at Beau Monde a while back. Sabrina's had a 2 hour wait so I convinced him to give BM another try. It didn't hurt I was able to make an opentable reservation, which guaranteed us a table in as short a wait as we could walk there from 10th + Christian. Knowing what I know now, I wish we had just turned around, gone home, and ate cereal. Thanks to our reservation, we were seated somewhat immediately. (FYI: If you're not so fortunate, and it happens to be cold/raining/snowing/scorching hot/etc. be prepared for the elements--there is no where to wait inside.) We were seated at a table directly behind and to the right of the hostess stand. It was fine until the only table next to us got up and they relocated it to the other side of the room. This left our table of two floating in the middle of the restaurant. This wouldn't have been so bad, except for the irony. Every server, bus person, and hostess had to dance around our table--yet no one ever looked down to see we were being completely ignored. Once our server finally approached our table (a solid 15 minutes later) our greeting was "Can I take your food order?" No apology for the delay and apparently we're skipping past coffee/tea/juice and going straight to the $20 crepe order. I was firm in my request for hot tea and he was so annoyed he just ordered water. We obviously knew what we wanted to order since we had an opportunity to read the menu 25 times over. I wish instead of saying "crepe with mixed berries" I had said "forget it" and we'd gotten up and left. But then I would have missed the best part--when she came back with my tea! As she held the cow-shaped-creamer by its' curled tail handle, the awkward, top heavy shape caused her to spill its' entire contents almost the entire trip to our deserted island--all over the floor, up my leg and on my shoes. Cue the irony that I don't even use cream in my tea....! Admittedly, it was an accident though and those are 100% forgivable in my book. Our crepes were delivered by a busser/expediter and no one ever came and asked "how is everything". My tea went empty until I had 1 bite remaining and we left shaking our heads at an utterly TERRIBLE experience--feeling poor and hungry still! In the end, there was no "Thank you", "Come Again", or "Have a great day". She simply took my credit card, rang it up, and redelivered the billfold. I couldn't help but think "is the waitstaff here salaried???" Look...we are not monsters. We are really reasonable people who understand and totally appreciate a busy brunch spot in this city. We're patient! We really are! And although we're usually all about forgiveness, this was one experience that has has us both crossing Beau Monde off the list for good. I'm not out to put anyone out of business, but the truth is--save yourself the trouble! Thanks but no thanks, Beau Monde. We will NOT be returning. P.S. If by some stroke of luck our server is out there reading this --I need you to know that if it weren't for my insufferable guilt you would have been TOTALLY justifiable in a stiffing. :/

text: These other reviews are, in my opinion, a false representation of how good this restaurant really is. I've eaten here several times over the last 4 years so let me explain.... I typically try to give a history lesson on a restaurant if I have one but in this case, what I know is not much. Their claim is that they have been cooking Cuban cuisine in the city since 1969. It is entirely family owned. The husband and wife work the kitchen, the children work the dining tables and the grandfather operates the bar. There is still a bit of a language barrier when speaking to the restaurant staff or placing orders. I think, due to this, staff prefer not to communicate with customers much more than they have to. This shouldn't detract from the overall experience, however. I mean, it's all about the food, isn't it? Initial entry into the restaurant, I'll admit, is a little dark. It's floor-plan is very much like a shotgun house in that it runs deep, not wide and spacious. There are no windows in the joint except for those at the front of the restaurant, near the bar. The décor is very dated and the walls have been painted, depicting various tropical scenes. I had read an earlier review where a customer referred to the interior is being much like a "compound" of sorts. This is accurate, due to the deficiency of outside light. Again, this isn't quite enough to ruin a good meal. This restaurant also makes a bulk of their income from the lunch crowd. At noon, the place is filled with suits and there is plenty of hustle and bustle. At dinner time, the place is a ghost town. The food quality remains as strong as ever, though. My favorite dishes in the restaurant are the Flank Steak and the Ropa Vieja. The Flank Steak dish is served with black beans, rice and fried sweet plantains. The seasoning of this steak is perfect! I've tried to mimic the flavors at my own home and I'm always missing something. I do detect black pepper, garlic and lemon. It's just an awesome combination of flavors and expertly executed! The Rope Vieja is another wonderful dish of thinly shredded beef that's seasoned with red wine, tomato sauce, garlic and bell peppers. Black beans, rice and fried sweet plantains are also served, however I do believe they change up the sides on this dish from time to time. The plantains always remain, though, and rightfully so. I can't so enough about the plantains in here. OMG, they are just so terrific! Now, let's review: the restaurant is a little pricey. However, each dish is very large so you can't complain about the portions. The dishes are also always precisely prepared so you're paying for quality. Yes, the restaurant is not very lively in the evenings but think of that as a good thing. If you want to have an intimate conversation with a date, this is a good place to go. If you've been around noise all day and long for quiet, this is a good place to go. If you're just looking for some good food for dinner, this is a good place to go! Also, make sure to try the mojitos from the bar! This restaurant makes the BEST mojitos in the city, bar none! About 4 years ago, this restaurant showed up in a New Orleans publication as being rated #1 for mojitos. Since that time, the title of "#1" has changed hands several times but in my opinion, this restaurant still holds the title. Do yourself a favor and check this restaurant out!

text: My experience with this race got off to a shaky start when I had trouble getting my husband registered with the "military discount". On the Active website, there was just one question - "Are you active military?" Well, he isn't...so I said no. When I brought it up to race director Rusty Snow on the race's Facebook page that the registration was confusing, he just told me he was sorry I missed the discount when registering. When I pressed on the issue because other former military folks were also not getting the discount, I was verbally hassled on the FB page by Rusty's friends. WTH? All I was trying to do was make sure all of the veterans were getting their registration discount. Anyway...my husband and I flew in from Dallas, TX. I'm a UCSB alum ('93), so the area is pretty familiar to me. I will agree the expo wasn't anything to write home about, but it's a small race so it didn't bug me too much...my expectations were pretty low. I did think the race shirts were pretty chintzy, given how great they looked last year. I asked a woman at the "information desk" at which bus area at UCSB we'd be meeting the shuttles (there are two, BTW), she simply quoted the website to me which just said "the bus rotunda". Okay. We did drive as much of the course as we could beforehand, so we knew going in how far off the elevation chart was from the website. The elevation chart shows the course as pretty much being all downhill the first 6 miles. Wrong. It's downhill, then uphill, then downhill. Makes a difference. Like Shannon N., I was appalled at what a complete clusterfu&k the shuttle situation was at UCSB. We were there at 6 AM and didn't board a bus until 6:55 AM...and, there were literally hundreds of people behind us waiting for a seat on one of the two paltry buses they had chartered for the event. It didn't help matters that cute little college girls who had no idea what they were doing were coordinating the bus effort on campus. Acting giddy and stupid and clueless may work when school is in session, but no one around me was amused. By the time we got to the Page Youth Center, we had just barely enough time to go to the bathroom and drop our bags before the race started. They did delay the start 15 minutes and we were lucky we got to start "on time". I was highly annoyed there wasn't a single water station until 3.6 miles in, and even at that one there was maybe half a table of cups of water with just a tiny amount of water in each cup. The lady pouring the water (only two people there, NICE) kept getting interrupted by running/racing friends stopping to give her hugs. I thought that was really inappropriate, because a ton of people were coming through and there wasn't enough water. Another gripe about the aid stations - while the people were friendly, the electrolyte beverage and water were mixed at the stations, so I had to yell at people working to find out what they had. The cups were the same, so it was very confusing to find what I was looking for. Probably the weirdest thing was after I finished the big hill on Cliff Drive...I was walking (hey, I was tired) and a young woman in a reflective vest came out onto the course next to me and proceeded to jog along with me to the next aid station. I'm not sure if these folks were told to do that if they saw someone walking? I wasn't in distress...I was just walking. It was strange. I didn't feel like socializing, and I wasn't in any physical trouble. Finally...the finish line. After running over 2 hours in the sun and warm temps, all I wanted was a bottle of water...and I HAD TO HUNT FOR ONE. Seriously? There needed to be a person handing me a bottle of water at the same time someone handed me my medal. I shouldn't have to walk a quarter of the way around the track with what seemed like 5,000 other people just to get some damn water. Seems like the entire run, all I was trying to do was get some water. And finally...the nail in the coffin...the shuttle bus back to UCSB. The woman driving the bus didn't seem to know what she was supposed to do, or where she was supposed to go. It didn't help that half the people on our bus were trying to get her to drop them off at the start line, where I guess they had left their cars. Next time, have the drivers announce before they leave that they are going to UCSB and UCSB only. Short story, long...I won't run this again. While I had a great run, it was far from a great race. Rusty Snow et. al. really need to work on the challenges that come with running a race of this scale.
label: NEG

text: Totally downgraded to "meh." I've been here about ten times since they've opened 6 months ago, so I speak from continued experience. The food is fine - not great, but fine. If you eat in, they don't time your meals to come out together (think: hot sandwiches on table at 6:30 and calzones at 6:45.) Clean restaurant, generally not busy, good burgers, decent pizza (better than Plaza) but not good cheesesteak, sadly. BF says, "I CANNOT believe that 'cheesesteak' is in their name - shameful." This happened to me here for the fist time ever - my called-in pizza order not even prepared or in the oven until I arrived to pick it up (I was 5 - 10 minutes late, store was not busy, plenty of staff.) The mistake was not acknowledged - I just had to sit and watch as my pizza was created and cooked while being told, "it's almost done - it's almost ready - just another minute." I would have been totally fine with a simple "oops! we forgot!" - I could have run next door to CVS for milk or something to pass the time - but I was so burned that they made me sit there for 15 minutes that I vowed never to return. Well, two months passed, my irritation cooled, we got a text ad for $5 pizzas and we decided to give it another go for a cheap takeout dinner. Guess what? SAME THING HAPPENED. When I figured it out, I just sat there, so angry that I couldn't say a word. It was an empty restaurant - was totally awkward to just stare at them - and I couldn't wait to get out of there. I just decided to complain by not giving them more of my money - and by downgrading my yelp review. Take that! It's a little sad, because we live and work literally around the corner, eat out 5 - 6 days a week, are patient customers and are regulars at other local restaurants. One particular owner has been there for most of my visits and he seems decent, and the staff is pleasant. But there's just so many other choices, and careless service just drives me crazy.

text: If you like to put a bird on it, this is the place for you. IHE happens once a year, and has grown from a lil' ol' craft show into a full-blown event with food, live acts, and booths upon booths of handmade goods, jewelry, trinkets, tschachkes, art, posters, toys, clothing...it is actually quite overwhelming with the amount of vendors they had this year. They have busted out of the Harrison Center and lined the streets with their non-traditional crafty goodness. No wooden American flags here! I think its great these artisans get to show off what they do to a large number of people, having the event the same day as the Talbot Street Art Fair is smart, smart, smart. But I almost think this should be a two day event, simply because for me, in all my ADD-ness, I really need one day to look around and soak everything in, process everything I've seen *then* go back and buy what I liked. There is just so much stuff and it is so spread out it is hard to decide what you really, really want. By the time I walked through the event and looked at everything, I had forgotten about whatever cool thing I was thinking about buying that I had seen earlier while wandering around. I also really enjoy the people watching - this thing attracts more hipsters than you can shake a stick at, you could capture a month's worth of photos to upload to http://www.latfh.com/.

text: I've never reviewed Santucci's?!?! Wow. This is our go-to pizza place. Only most of the time, we don't go, we just order. Their delivery has always been fast and accurate. The square pizza is definitely unique in that the crust is much thinner than a typical Sicilian pie and it is topped with a thin layer of mozzarella first, and zesty sauce on top of that. The best topping we've tried is the sausage. It has a great flavor and always gets slightly crisp on top. Meatball pies are great too, but the meatballs have a distinct spice to them, something along the lines of nutmeg. So if that's not your thing, take note. text: After discovering that Buona Vita is apparently out of business (we had a gift certificate we were trying to use), my husband and I, with our heads still focused on an italian dinner, went to nearby Primi Urban Cafe instead. Despite this there was only one waiter on duty. There was a runner who was also filling waters, but when the waiter, Simon I think his name was, stopped to greet us he was visibly rushed and there were long waits between his visits. He sped through the specials, disappeared for ten minutes, returned and sped through our orders. To his credit, he did seem to be getting everyone what they needed, and since we are currently on a tight budget, we did not order drinks or appetizers so there wasn't a whole lot to screw up in our order. And the food was wonderful. I ordered the Pasta el Limone with fettucini and it was heavenly! Indulgently creamy and rich with parmesan flavor, cut with a nice lemon and white wine tang. Decadent was the word I thought as I was eating it and wondering how much was going to go straight to my hips. Oh but it was worth it! The pasta itself was as perfect as pasta gets. Soft and clean, with just the right firmness and clearly made either onsite or nearby. My husband ordered the Angry Pasta - which is just your choice of pasta in red sauce that is supposed to contain some chili for heat. Brian's sauce was definitely not spicy, which is the whole reason he ordered it, but the sauce was still so yummy that he was not disappointed enough to send it back... or to stop groaning from pleasure with every bite. Truly it was some of the best pasta I have ever had. We did get the creme brule dessert to share and it was good, however cold. Including the burnt sugar on the top, which is a clear sign that they premake their desserts and keep them refrigerated. Besides that, the biggest downside was that I was hoping I would come home with some leftovers for lunch the next day, but despite the portion size I just couldn't stop eating and pretty much cleaned my plates. The atmosphere was very warm, with a live piano player, a heavily perfumed manager/owner (?) standing at attention at all time ensuring good service (and honestly, we did wait a little but we really had nothing pressing to do that evening, and he was visibly rushed, but having waited tables before I can only give kudos to Simon for his cool, speed and proficiency with such a huge work load), there are several tvs above the bar which gave it a casual touch that didn't really match the quality of the food, but being a child of the media age I didn't mind this as much as some others might. We will definitely be returning to this place, especially considering that I can't get that amazing Lemon pasta out of my mind! And please be sure to tip well your hardworking server!!

The bacon and the BBQ sauce were good complements to the tenderness of the scallop meat. 3) The cioppino was good. Offered a good amount of crab, although only 3 of the legs remained. However, the ones we ate in San Francisco were much better. The bad: 1) clam chowder - was good, but lacked the freshness. Also wasn't as piping hot as it should be when it first comes out to the table. The lobster deal on Tuesday and Wednesday was the best deal, hands down. They also offer a 2 lb. text: Went to Hamburger Mary's for their Grand Opening party on a Saturday night. The place was really getting packed and we had to park down the street. We got drinks and waited on our table...which only took about 30 minutes. All the staff was super nice which they should be on opening night, but it was sooo crazy busy that I could see them being a bit rushed with us but they were not that way at all. We decided to try some of their "Special-Teases" on the drink menu and got them "Mary Size" which was a huge 22oz!! We got a Mary's Fruit Punch which was cherry, raspberry and grape vodkas mixed with cranberry and pink lemonade. YUMMY!!! These are great to split btw. Our quesadilla came out for our starter and I did like that they used different types of tortillas, but otherwise it was average. Very tasty, but kinda thin and just regular. The place looks very cool and has a definite "Retro" feel to it which I'm sure is intentional. There are even 45s on the wall behind the DJ station. There are 2 levels and the upper level has a more intimate, casual feel to it where you can just hang and watch tv if that's your thing. The lower level is very spacious and there is a stage on one end and this night we got to listen to Kim Massie sing (which is always a treat). Later there was to be a Drag show but that will have to wait for another visit. Great burgers and a fun place....maybe a tad bit pricey for the burgers, but they are really big. I think this would be a great spot to bring a group of friends.....anyone? P.S. They do have a parking lot next to the restaurant....THIS IS A PAY AHEAD LOT. You put the money in the little slots. My friends went here after us and parked there but they said they saw no signs that told them to pay. When they went back to their car they had a ticket for 15.00!!! text: We had stumbled upon this restaurant while walking around the city. We love spicy food, especially Sichuan cuisine, and the prices were right so we decided to give it a try. The staff were very friendly and attentive and as someone who previously lived in China for over six years I can say that the Sichuan food was quite authentic. We did not try anything off the fusion menu except for a complementary Ahi Tuna appetizer which was very good, but as for the Sichuan food we felt everything was on point. We ordered the dry pepper chicken, the mapo tofu, and the dan dan noodles. The dan dan was not the best we've had in Philly (we liked Han Dynasty's better) but was very good nonetheless. The mapo tofu was one of the best we've ever tasted, while the pepper chicken was good albiet having a different texture from what we are normally accustomed to. Regarding the "unpleasant" numbing feeling from certain dishes another reviewer has described, this sensation comes from the Sichuan peppercorn which is an essential and defining component of many authentic Sichuanese dishes (known in China as "ma la", literally "numbing spicy") and we enjoyed it very much! We will definitely be returning in the near future - although we came for dinner the lunch menu's prices were especially attractive, and we highly recommend it if you are in town looking for some authentic Chinese cuisine!

The only really big problem I had with this dish was the tortilla chips. They were elastically which most probably meant they weren't fried long enough. So there wasn't really a crunch but more of a bite and shake your head and hands to get it to rip. The price is reasonable for this meal and I'd highly recommend it to anyone who is within the area to try. PS: If you want to know what your crab looks like before you eat--you can walk in to check it out. They're in huge fish tanks! PPS: Remember to sign your name on the wait-list and be present when they call you!

However, these things are part of the authentic pho experience, to me -- lots of sauces on the formica tables, plenty of napkins, and mom and pop in the kitchen cooking. Decoration takes a backseat to food here. The rolls are excellent, not relying too heavily on rice noodles for filler, using lettuce and bright mint instead. Try the shrimp, Chinese sausage, and egg rolls! They're a wonderful riff on traditional goi cuon. Pho Bac also serves a variety of drinks other than the standard water, soda, and hot tea. The iced Vietnamese coffee is delicious. Excellent food, authentic atmosphere -- absolutely five stars from me.
